sections: Fit the carton to the bottle and cap

Start with the filled bottle that will reach the packing line. Record the tallest cap and the widest point across the glass, including shoulders and any label seam. A nominal capacity such as 15 mL tells the buyer how much liquid the bottle holds. A drawing or a sample bottle gives the converter the shape needed to make the carton. If the same bottle has brush-cap options, send the tallest and widest combinations you intend to pack. A bottle should slip past the dust flaps without scraping the label or pulling on the cap. Check the same movement when removing it. If it rattles or leans, compare a closer-fitting carton with a small board cradle before adding a more complex insert.
Choose a tuck end that suits your packing bench

The reference shows a top tuck opening with side tabs. Ask the factory to show both ends on the structural drawing, and agree on the loading end before artwork begins. A tuck flap should close flush after loading without pressing on the cap. For a multi-shade order, make a short trial with the actual filling team. Ask the operator to form, load and close several samples in sequence. If a bottom tab catches the bottle or the closing flap backs out, fix the flap or the loading sequence while the dieline can still change. Fold the carton around a real bottle to check for a straight front when the unit stands upright.
Build a shade system for the full printed front

Use one consistent position for the shade name and collection identity so retail staff can scan a row of cartons quickly. Dusty rose is the design direction for this reference. If the artwork needs to match a brand guide or a color swatch, provide a physical reference and identify which elements change with each shade. An ink drawdown or a printed proof on the intended stock helps you judge whether two neighboring shades still read as different. Review the folded sample, especially where a wraparound line meets an edge or the tuck panel. A consistent side-panel layout also helps identify products when boxes are stored on their sides.
Lay out back-panel copy before proof approval

Map your rear and side panels early so the artwork designer can see how much flat area is available. Place the barcode on an uninterrupted panel clear of creases, glue and heavy graphics. Ask for a printed scan check on any barcode that will be used in the final packaging. The ingredient copy and codes in the reference images are examples of placement. Supply your own approved content for each destination, including any variant-specific data. For repeat production, label each file with its product code and revision so the packing team can match the carton to the right bottle.
Approve the filled sample before ordering by shade

Try the bottle upright and on its side under ordinary handling. Observe movement, closure engagement and whether the front panel bows. For parcel orders, evaluate the retail carton inside the intended shipper, including any dividers or cushioning. Once fit is approved, record the common dieline, paperboard and artwork per shade. Send your receiving country and order split so the quote can identify production quantities by design. See the comparison with the {related} if buyers need to see the bottle itself on the shelf.
faq: Can different shades share a carton dieline?
Yes, provided their bottles, caps and packing method fit the same approved structure. Give each printed variant its own artwork reference and quantity.
Do I need an internal support for one bottle?
A close-fitting carton can be assessed first. Add a board support if the bottle moves excessively, loads awkwardly or needs more clearance around the cap.
Is the shown 15 mL bottle size fixed?
No. It is the reference design shown in the images. Carton dimensions follow your bottle and approved sample.

sections: Decide what shoppers need to see

A cutout can show the polish through the glass, a shade sticker or a label on the bottle. Give the engineer a front-view photo of the bottle and mark the portion to keep visible. Rectangular bottles can have a substantial glass shoulder or base that makes the same color look lighter around the edges. Place the opening to show the area that reads most clearly. Check the result from the distance expected at a shop display and again at a shallow angle. If the cap fills most of the opening, move the window or adjust the seating height instead of making the hole larger by default.
Keep usable board around the window

Choose the cutout size with the body panel and folds in mind. A window that comes too close to a crease can leave a thin strip of board that distorts when the carton is erected. Ask for a plain structural sample in the proposed board. Open and close several units, check the corner of the opening for damage and see whether the front stays flat around the bottle. If a display needs a window patch, confirm the film option, where it goes on the inside and how its seam sits away from the visible area. The cutout is visible in the reference image. Patch material and thickness are project choices.
Keep the bottle facing the customer

A well-positioned hole helps only while the bottle stays aligned behind it. Show the factory where the bottle label and cap should sit and whether the bottle front can rotate. Use the filled bottle during sample review and check a few handling positions that match your packing and shelving. If it drifts, test a paperboard locator or a revised internal fit. Confirm that any support can be folded and loaded consistently by the packing team. For several shades in one collection, try both the lightest and darkest bottles so you can see whether the artwork, opening and glass still work together.
Review the artwork on an erected carton

Keep the shade name readable even where the actual polish color is visible. Customers may still use the printed name to compare a swatch chart with the product on the shelf. Reserve a separate area for a store label if your retailer adds one. Keep the optical center of the logo, window and bottle front aligned on the built sample. Review the cutting edge next to fine printed lines and keep important copy away from the cut. You can compare the {related} if different sales channels need a full brand panel or more room for artwork.
Brief the factory with one complete display reference

Send bottle dimensions including the cap, filled weight, a front photo, window outline, SKU quantities and intended shelf or counter display. If the carton may travel through parcel fulfillment, share the outer pack plan so the front window can be assessed in context. The final proof should identify what is printed and what is cut. Check the packed sample for cut edge quality, bottle position, removal and any patch glare before release. Record the winning bottle and cutout position together so artwork variations do not alter the approved display layout.
faq: Can the window be left open?
An open cutout or a patched window can be reviewed. Select one based on retail handling and the appearance of a packed sample.
Can I display several shades using one window layout?
Yes, if bottle shape and label position are consistent. Check the visible area with the intended shade and label variants.
Will a window automatically keep the bottle in place?
The cutout provides visibility. The internal fit or a locating insert determines how the bottle sits behind it.

sections: Plan the order in which the pair is revealed

Decide which bottle appears first as the drawer moves out. A color pair may be arranged from lighter to darker, whereas a base-and-topcoat kit may follow application order. Give the printer and the packing team the same orientation reference. If the buyer expects bottles to be read upright while the box is open, set cavity orientation before position marks or shade names are put on the tray. Use the approved drawing to identify the opening side. If you want a pull ribbon or notch, show where a finger can reach without touching the bottle. The reference illustrates the sliding structure without confirming any added pull hardware.
Test a loaded drawer inside its actual sleeve

The nominal outside dimensions alone cannot capture what the drawer feels like. Load the two filled bottles and slide the tray in using the intended grip point. Note whether resistance appears throughout the travel or only near the fully closed position. Review sleeve squareness, tray fit and the height of the bottle caps if the drawer catches. If the empty drawer travels smoothly and the loaded drawer catches, check if a cap sits proud or the insert lifts when loaded. Use the intended wrap thickness on the final sample. A paper change can affect how the two parts move against one another.
Keep the bottles separated and simple to remove

Compare the body width, shoulder transition and cap shape of both bottles. Two bottles of the same capacity can require different cavities. Give the tray designer an actual bottle for each position, plus a target removal point. A relief near the bottle body can make it easier to lift square glass without levering against its cap. Check that the middle divider leaves enough material to stay intact during normal loading and that the second bottle stays seated when the first is removed. Keep the insert material open until the sample confirms fit and appearance.
Specify shared sleeves and distinct pair artwork

A shared sleeve can simplify replenishment if pair names are assigned on a separate panel or label area. Directly printed pair artwork may make more sense when combinations have distinct retail identities. Map each pair to a product code and quantity, then decide whether the insert and body remain common. Review the back and front together with the actual distribution labels. Do I need to sample the sleeve and tray together?
Yes. Review them as a loaded set so you can check slide resistance, cover clearance and how far the drawer should travel.
Can the same packaging serve more than one duo?
It can if the bottle profiles and approved cavity positions match. Keep the artwork and set coding separate by pairing.

Make sure walls between cavities separate the bottles in ordinary handling and let the packing team seat each bottle without forcing it. sections: Treat the inside lid as a presentation panel

The lid stays with the base while the shopper sees the collection. It can carry a short collection title, product routine or shade order if the brief calls for it. Keep critical artwork away from the hinge and fold area. Review how the text reads when the lid is held at a normal opening angle rather than when the artwork is laid flat. Work the lid normally with the case empty. Check that it sits square on the base and opens smoothly. Then place the insert and repeat the check before loading the four bottles.
